lesson.title: No Function Can Run Forever: The Extreme Value Theorem
lesson.summary: The Extreme Value Theorem guarantees that a function which is continuous on a closed interval must attain both a highest value and a lowest value somewhere on that interval.
lesson.body:
Picture a hiking trail that starts at a trailhead, ends at a lookout point, and has no breaks, cliffs, or teleporters along the way. Common sense says the trail must have some highest elevation and some lowest elevation, and you must actually stand at those spots at some point during the hike. That common sense observation, made rigorous, is the Extreme Value Theorem, one of the most useful existence guarantees in all of calculus.

The theorem states: if f is a continuous function on a closed interval [a, b], then f attains a global maximum value at some point c in [a, b], and f attains a global minimum value at some point d in [a, b]. In plain language, the function does not just get close to a highest or lowest value, it actually reaches those values, and it does so at specific input values inside the interval, including possibly the endpoints themselves.

It is worth being precise about what this theorem promises and what it does not promise. It promises existence: a highest point and a lowest point are guaranteed to be there. It says nothing about how to find them, how many times each value is attained, or what the function looks like in between. Finding the actual locations c and d is a separate job, one that the rest of this chapter builds the tools for.

Here is the guarantee in action. Let f(x) = x^2 on the closed interval [-1, 3]. This function is a polynomial, so it is continuous everywhere, and [-1, 3] is closed and bounded, so both hypotheses of the theorem are satisfied. The Extreme Value Theorem guarantees a global max and global min both exist somewhere in [-1, 3], before we do a single calculation.

Now locate them. The graph of x^2 is a parabola opening upward with its lowest point at x = 0, and x = 0 falls inside [-1, 3], so f(0) = 0 is a candidate for the minimum. The only other places a global extreme value could hide on a closed interval are the two endpoints, so evaluate there too: f(-1) = 1, and f(3) = 9. Comparing the three candidate values 0, 1, and 9, the smallest is 0 at x = 0, and the largest is 9 at x = 3. So the global minimum value is 0, attained at x = 0, and the global maximum value is 9, attained at x = 3, exactly as the theorem promised would exist.

This pattern, checking the interior turning points of the graph alongside the two endpoints, is the standard strategy for actually locating global extrema once you know the Extreme Value Theorem guarantees they exist. The next several sections turn this informal idea of an interior turning point into a precise, searchable definition.
